newsitem.title: BURKINA FASO: Africa's top film festival begins.
newsitem.headline: Africa's top film festival begins.

text.p: Africa's top film festival began in Burkina Faso's capital Ouagadougou on Saturday, attended by film makers or talent spotters from across the continent and Europe and the United States.

The biennial Ouagadougou PanAfrican Festival of Cinema and Television (FESPACO), launched with an opening ceremony at the capital's August 4 stadium, takes as this year's theme Cinema, Childhood and Youth.

The undercurrent running through the week-long festival is how to respond to an onslaught of Hollywood blockbusters and foreign action films that dominate the continent's cinema and television screens.

"If Africans are watching foreign films, it's because the rhythm at which African films come out is so slow," director Idrissa Ouedraogo, from Burkina Faso, told weekly magazine Jeune Afrique in a special supplement on the festival.

"We must help Africa to tell her own story because no-one can do it better," director Gaston Kabore, also from Burkina Faso, told a meeting of the PanAfrican Federation of Film makers (FEPACI) before the main opening.
Kabore, one of those competing for the top prize, is due to stand down after 12 years at the head of the federation.

Burkina Faso's culture and communication minister had a similar message, urging FEPACI to promote training and the distribution and showing of African films and South-South cooperation on productions. "FEPACI must at all costs continue to show the way forward, wake people up, organise get-togethers, propose strategies," Mahamoudou Ouedraogo said.
A total of 19 feature films from 11 African countries are competing for the main honour at FESPACO '97 -- the coveted Etalon de Yennenga (Yennenga Stallion) awarded to the best film.
The figure is down on the 23 films in the 1995 festival but the organisers say that this reflects their concern to maintain the high professional standards of the festival, first held in 1969.
Films in the competition include "Waati" by Malian director Souleymane Cisse, which featured at France's prestigious Cannes Film Festival and tells the story of a South African in exile.
Others include Kabore's "Buud Yam", "Un Ete a La Goulette" (A Summer in Goulette) by Tunisian Ferid Boughedir and "Salut Cousin" (Hi Cousin) by Algerian Merzak Allouache.
Mali and Tunisia are the best represented with three films each. Other countries represented include Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Zaire, Cape Verde, Guinea and Senegal.
Egypt, which arguably boasts the continent's biggest film industry, was not represented.
The festival offers competitions for short films and documentaries (26 entries) and TV and video films (25 entries).

A market of 400 stalls has sprung up in the city centre to serve the needs of the estimated 3,500 festival goers. This year for the first time, the organisers plan to public screenings of films, including those in competition, on Revolution Square.
But outside reality -- in the form of a dispute between the government and students over allowances and conditions -- threatens to intrude.
The students have called for a march on Monday. The city mayor has banned it, saying FESPACO cannot be disrupted.
